title: Ethiopian Sesame Brittle
community: Ethiopian markets and street vendors — the sesame sweet
author: Mama Tigist
desc: Ethiopian Sesame Brittle — sesame seeds caramelised in honey and set into thin, crispy sheets. The Ethiopian sweet street candy — sold at every market in thin slabs, an ancient confection made from Ethiopia's two most precious produce: sesame and honey.
longDesc: Ethiopian sesame brittle is the oldest candy in Ethiopia — sesame has been cultivated in Ethiopia for thousands of years and honey is one of the country's most important products. Together they produce a confection of remarkable simplicity and satisfaction.
steps: Toast sesame seeds in a dry pan over medium heat — 3 minutes until golden.
Add honey, sugar, and salt. Stir continuously.
Cook over medium heat 5—6 minutes until the mixture turns deep golden.
It should reach the hard crack stage (150°C).
Quickly pour onto lined baking sheet.
Spread thin with an oiled spatula.
chefTips: Speed is essential at the pouring stage — the brittle sets quickly.
The hard crack stage (150°C) is where the sugar becomes brittle when cooled.
Oil your spatula before spreading — the mixture sticks aggressively.
commonMistakes: Not reaching hard crack temperature — sticky rather than brittle.
cookingScience: At 150°C (hard crack stage), virtually all the water has evaporated from the sugar mixture and the sucrose has undergone significant inversion. When cooled, this low-water sugar matrix solidifies into an amorphous glass — the brittle snap comes from the absence of water crystalline structure.
sustainabilityTips: Ethiopian sesame from Tigray and Humera — one of the world's finest sesame regions.
healthBenefits: Sesame is very high in calcium and zinc.
High in healthy fats from sesame.
culturalNote: Ethiopian sesame brittle is the market sweet that connects present-day Ethiopia to its ancient past — sesame cultivation in Ethiopia predates recorded history, and the combination of sesame and honey has been a sweet for millennia. Buying a piece from a market vendor wrapping it in newsprint is a sensory experience that connects to centuries of Ethiopian market life.
